{{Short description|Criterion in quantum information theory}}
{{Use American English|date = February 2019}}
{{Use mdy dates|date = February 2019}}

The '''Peres–Horodecki criterion''' is a necessary condition, for the joint [[density matrix]] <math>\rho</math> of two quantum mechanical systems <math>A</math> and <math>B</math>, to be [[separable states|separable]]. It is also called the '''PPT''' criterion, for ''positive partial transpose''. In the 2×2 and 2×3 dimensional cases the condition is also sufficient. It is used to decide the separability of [[Mixed state (physics)|mixed state]]s, where the [[Schmidt decomposition#Schmidt rank and entanglement|Schmidt decomposition]] does not apply. The theorem was discovered in 1996 by [[Asher Peres]]<ref>{{Cite journal|last=Peres|first=Asher|date=1996-08-19|title=Separability Criterion for Density Matrices|url=https://link.aps.org/doi/10.1103/PhysRevLett.77.1413|journal=Physical Review Letters|language=en|volume=77|issue=8|pages=1413–1415|doi=10.1103/PhysRevLett.77.1413|pmid=10063072 |arxiv=quant-ph/9604005|bibcode=1996PhRvL..77.1413P |s2cid=5246518 }}</ref> and the Horodecki family ([[Michał Horodecki|Michał]], [[Paweł Horodecki|Paweł]], and [[Ryszard Horodecki|Ryszard]])<ref>{{Cite journal|last1=Horodecki|first1=Michał|last2=Horodecki|first2=Paweł|last3=Horodecki|first3=Ryszard|date=1996|title=Separability of mixed states: necessary and sufficient conditions|url=https://linkinghub.elsevier.com/retrieve/pii/S0375960196007062|journal=Physics Letters A|language=en|volume=223|issue=1–2|pages=1–8|doi=10.1016/S0375-9601(96)00706-2|arxiv=quant-ph/9605038|bibcode=1996PhLA..223....1H |s2cid=10580997 }}</ref>

In higher dimensions, the test is inconclusive, and one should supplement it with more advanced tests, such as those based on [[entanglement witness]]es.

==Definition==

If we have a general state <math>\rho</math> which acts on [[Hilbert space]] of <math>\mathcal{H}_A \otimes \mathcal{H}_B</math>

:<math>\rho = \sum_{ijkl} p^{ij}_{kl} |i\rangle \langle j | \otimes |k\rangle \langle l| </math>

Its partial [[transpose]] (with respect to the B party) is defined as

:<math>\rho^{T_B} := (I \otimes T) (\rho) = \sum_{ijkl} p^{ij} _{kl} |i\rangle \langle j | \otimes (|k\rangle \langle l|)^T = \sum_{ijkl} p^{ij} _{kl} |i\rangle \langle j | \otimes |l\rangle \langle k| = \sum_{ijkl} p^{ij} _{lk} |i\rangle \langle j | \otimes |k\rangle \langle l|</math>

Note that the ''partial'' in the name implies that only part of the state is transposed. More precisely, <math> (I \otimes T) (\rho) </math> is the identity [[linear map|map]] applied to the A party and the transposition map applied to the B party.

This definition can be seen more clearly if we write the state as a [[block matrix]]:

:<math>\rho = \begin{pmatrix} A_{11} & A_{12} & \dots & A_{1n} \\ A_{21} & A_{22} & & \\ \vdots & & \ddots & \\ A_{n1} & & & A_{nn} \end{pmatrix}</math>

Where <math>n = \dim \mathcal{H}_A</math>, and each block is a [[square matrix]] of dimension <math>m = \dim \mathcal{H}_B</math>. Then the partial transpose is

:<math>\rho^{T_B} = \begin{pmatrix} A_{11}^T & A_{12}^T & \dots & A_{1n}^T \\ A_{21}^T & A_{22}^T & & \\ \vdots & & \ddots & \\ A_{n1}^T & & & A_{nn}^T \end{pmatrix}</math>

The criterion states that if <math>\rho\;\!</math> is separable then all the [[eigenvalues]] of <math>\rho^{T_B}</math> are non-negative. In other words, if <math>\rho^{T_B}</math> has a negative eigenvalue, <math>\rho\;\!</math> is guaranteed to be [[Quantum entanglement|entangled]]. The converse of these statements is true [[if and only if]] the dimension of the product space is <math> 2 \times 2</math> or <math> 2 \times 3</math>.

The result is independent of the party that was transposed, because <math>\rho^{T_A} = (\rho^{T_B})^T</math>.

==Example==

Consider this 2-qubit family of [[Werner state]]s:

:<math>\rho = p |\Psi^-\rangle \langle \Psi^-| + (1-p) \frac{I}{4} </math>

It can be regarded as the [[convex combination]] of <math>|\Psi^-\rangle</math>, a [[maximally entangled state]], 
and the [[identity element]], a [[maximally mixed state]].

Its density matrix is

:<math>\rho = \frac{1}{4}\begin{pmatrix}
1-p & 0 & 0 & 0\\
0 & p+1 & -2p & 0\\
0 & -2p & p+1 & 0 \\
0 & 0 & 0 & 1-p\end{pmatrix}</math>

and the partial transpose

:<math>\rho^{T_B} = \frac{1}{4}\begin{pmatrix}
1-p & 0 & 0 & -2p\\
0 & p+1 & 0 & 0\\
0 & 0 & p+1 & 0 \\
-2p & 0 & 0 & 1-p\end{pmatrix}</math>

Its least eigenvalue is <math>(1-3p)/4</math>. Therefore, the state is entangled for <math> 1 \geq p > 1/3 </math>.

==Demonstration==

If ρ is separable, it can be written as

:<math> \rho = \sum p_i \rho^A_i \otimes \rho^B_i </math>

In this case, the effect of the partial transposition is trivial:

:<math>\rho^{T_B} = (I \otimes T )(\rho) = \sum p_i \rho^A_i \otimes (\rho^B_i)^T </math>

As the transposition map preserves eigenvalues, the spectrum of <math>(\rho^B_i)^{T}</math> is the same as the spectrum of <math>\rho^B_i\;\!</math>, and in particular <math>(\rho^B_i)^{T}</math> must still be positive semidefinite. Thus <math>\rho^{T_B}</math> must also be positive semidefinite. This proves the necessity of the PPT criterion.

Showing that being PPT is also sufficient for the 2 X 2 and 3 X 2 (equivalently 2 X 3) cases is more involved. It was shown by the Horodeckis that for every entangled state there exists an [[entanglement witness]]. This is a result of geometric nature and invokes the [[Hahn–Banach theorem]] (see reference below).

From the existence of entanglement witnesses, one can show that <math>I \otimes \Lambda (\rho) </math> being positive for all [[Choi's theorem on completely positive maps|positive maps]] Λ is a necessary and sufficient condition for the separability of ρ, where Λ maps <math> B(\mathcal{H}_B) </math> to <math>B(\mathcal{H}_A)</math>

Furthermore, every positive map from <math> B(\mathcal{H}_B) </math> to <math>B(\mathcal{H}_A)</math> can be decomposed into a sum of completely positive and completely copositive maps, when <math>\textrm{dim}(\mathcal{H}_B) = 2</math> and <math>\textrm{dim}(\mathcal{H}_A) = 2\;\textrm{or}\;3</math>. In other words, every such map Λ can be written as

:<math>\Lambda = \Lambda _1 + \Lambda _2 \circ T, </math>

where <math>\Lambda_1</math> and <math>\Lambda_2</math> are completely positive and ''T'' is the transposition map. This follows from the Størmer-Woronowicz theorem.

Loosely speaking, the transposition map is therefore the only one that can generate negative eigenvalues in these dimensions. So if <math>\rho^{T_B}</math> is positive, <math>I \otimes \Lambda (\rho) </math> is positive for any Λ. Thus we conclude that the Peres–Horodecki criterion is also sufficient for separability when <math>\textrm{dim}(\mathcal{H}_A \otimes \mathcal{H}_B) \le 6 </math>.

In higher dimensions, however, there exist maps that can't be decomposed in this fashion, and the criterion is no longer sufficient. Consequently, there are entangled states which have a positive partial transpose. Such states have the interesting property that they are [[Bound entanglement|bound entangled]], i.e. they can not be [[entanglement distillation|distilled]] for [[quantum communication]] purposes.

==Continuous variable systems==

The Peres–Horodecki criterion has been extended to continuous variable systems. [[Rajiah Simon]]<ref>{{cite journal|last1=Simon|first1=R.|title=Peres-Horodecki Separability Criterion for Continuous Variable Systems|journal=Physical Review Letters|volume=84|issue=12|pages=2726–2729|doi=10.1103/PhysRevLett.84.2726|arxiv = quant-ph/9909044 |bibcode = 2000PhRvL..84.2726S|pmid=11017310|year=2000|s2cid=11664720 }}</ref> formulated a particular version of the PPT criterion in terms of the second-order moments of canonical operators and showed that it is necessary and sufficient for <math> 1\oplus1 </math>-mode Gaussian states (see Ref.<ref>{{cite journal|last1=Duan|first1=Lu-Ming|last2=Giedke|first2=G.|last3=Cirac|first3=J. I.|last4=Zoller|first4=P.|title=Inseparability Criterion for Continuous Variable Systems|journal=Physical Review Letters|volume=84|issue=12|pages=2722–2725|doi=10.1103/PhysRevLett.84.2722|arxiv = quant-ph/9908056 |bibcode = 2000PhRvL..84.2722D|pmid=11017309|year=2000 |s2cid=9948874 }}</ref> for a seemingly different but essentially equivalent approach). It was later found <ref>{{cite journal|last1=Werner|first1=R. F.|last2=Wolf|first2=M. M.|title=Bound Entangled Gaussian States|journal=Physical Review Letters|volume=86|issue=16|pages=3658–3661|doi=10.1103/PhysRevLett.86.3658|arxiv = quant-ph/0009118 |bibcode = 2001PhRvL..86.3658W|pmid=11328047|year=2001 |s2cid=20897950 }}</ref> that Simon's condition is also necessary and sufficient for <math> 1\oplus n </math>-mode Gaussian states, but no longer sufficient for <math> 2\oplus2 </math>-mode Gaussian states. Simon's condition can be generalized by taking into account the higher order moments of canonical operators <ref>{{cite journal|last1=Shchukin|first1=E.|last2=Vogel|first2=W.|title=Inseparability Criteria for Continuous Bipartite Quantum States|journal=Physical Review Letters|volume=95|issue=23|doi=10.1103/PhysRevLett.95.230502|arxiv = quant-ph/0508132 |bibcode = 2005PhRvL..95w0502S|pmid=16384285|year=2005|article-number=230502 |s2cid=28595936 }}</ref><ref>{{cite journal|last1=Hillery|first1=Mark|last2=Zubairy|first2=M. Suhail|title=Entanglement Conditions for Two-Mode States|journal=Physical Review Letters|volume=96|issue=5|doi=10.1103/PhysRevLett.96.050503|arxiv = quant-ph/0507168 |bibcode = 2006PhRvL..96e0503H|pmid=16486912|article-number=050503|year=2006|s2cid=43756465 }}</ref> or by using entropic measures.<ref>{{cite journal|last1=Walborn|first1=S.|last2=Taketani|first2=B.|last3=Salles|first3=A.|last4=Toscano|first4=F.|last5=de Matos Filho|first5=R.|title=Entropic Entanglement Criteria for Continuous Variables|journal=Physical Review Letters|volume=103|issue=16|doi=10.1103/PhysRevLett.103.160505|arxiv = 0909.0147 |bibcode = 2009PhRvL.103p0505W|pmid=19905682|article-number=160505|year=2009|s2cid=10523704 }}</ref><ref>{{cite journal |last1=Yichen Huang |title=Entanglement Detection: Complexity and Shannon Entropic Criteria |journal=IEEE Transactions on Information Theory |date=October 2013 |volume=59 |issue=10 |pages=6774–6778 |doi=10.1109/TIT.2013.2257936|bibcode=2013ITIT...59.6774H |s2cid=7149863 }}</ref>

==Symmetric systems==

For symmetric states of bipartite systems, the positivity of the partial transpose of the density matrix is related to the sign of certain two-body correlations. Here, symmetry means that

:<math>\rho F_{AB}= F_{AB}\rho=\rho, </math>

holds, where <math>F_{AB}</math> is the flip or swap operator exchanging the two parties <math>A</math> and <math>B</math>. 
A full basis of the symmetric subspace is of the form <math>(\vert n\rangle_A \vert m \rangle_B + \vert m\rangle_A \vert n \rangle_B)/\sqrt{2}</math> with 
<math>m\ne n</math> and <math>\vert n\rangle_A \vert n \rangle_B.</math> Here for <math>n</math> and <math>m,</math> <math>0\le n,m \le d-1</math> must hold, where <math>d</math>
is the dimension of the two parties.

It can be shown that for such states, <math>\rho</math> has a positive partial transpose if and only if <ref>{{cite journal |last1=Tóth |first1=Géza |last2=Gühne |first2=Otfried |title=Entanglement and Permutational Symmetry |journal=Physical Review Letters |date=1 May 2009 |volume=102 |issue=17 |article-number=170503 |doi=10.1103/PhysRevLett.102.170503|pmid=19518768 |arxiv=0812.4453 |bibcode=2009PhRvL.102q0503T |s2cid=43527866 }}</ref>

:<math>\langle M \otimes M \rangle_\rho \ge 0 </math>

holds for all operators <math>M.</math> Hence, if <math>\langle M \otimes M \rangle_\rho < 0</math> holds for some <math>M</math> then the
state possesses non-PPT [[Quantum entanglement|entanglement]].

Moreover, a bipartite symmetric PPT state can be written as 
:<math>\varrho=\sum_k p_k M_k\otimes M_k,</math>
where <math>p_k</math> are probabilities and <math>M_k</math> fulfill 
<math>{\rm Tr}(M_k)=1</math>
and <math>{\rm Tr}(M_k^2)=1.</math>
However, for a subsystem larger than a qubit, <math>M_k</math> are not necessarily physical pure density matrices since they can have negative eigenvalues. In this case, even entangled states can be written as a mixture of tensor products of single-party aphysical states, very similar to the form of [[separable states]].
In the qubit case, <math>M_k</math> are physical density matrices, which is consistent with the fact that for two qubits all PPT states are separable.

The concept of such pseudomixtures has been extended to non-symmetric states and to the multipartite case, by the definition of pseudoseparable states<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Vitagliano |first1=Giuseppe |last2=Gühne |first2=Otfried |last3=Tóth |first3=Géza |title=s u ( d ) -squeezing and many-body entanglement geometry in finite-dimensional systems |journal=Quantum |date=3 September 2025 |volume=9 |article-number=1844 |doi=10.22331/q-2025-09-03-1844|arxiv=2406.13338 |bibcode=2025Quant...9.1844V }}</ref>
:<math>\varrho=\sum_k p_k M_k^{(1)}\otimes M_k^{(2)}\otimes ... \otimes M_k^{(N)},</math>
where <math>N</math> is the number of subsystems and <math>M_k^{(n)}</math>
fulfill <math>{\rm Tr}(M_k^{(n)})=1</math>
and <math>{\rm Tr}[(M_k^{(n)})^2]=1.</math>
The single subsystem aphysical states <math>M_k^{(n)}</math> are just states that live on the higher dimensional equivalent of the [[Bloch sphere]] even for systems that are larger than a qubit. Separable states are the subset of the set of pseudoseparable states, while for qubits the two sets coincide with each other. For systems larger than qubits, such quantum states can be entangled, and in this case they can have PPT or non-PPT bipartitions.
